docs/JBI_POSITIONING_AND_HYPOTHESES.md:11:### 1.1 Within-population polymorphism and among-population differentiation are biologically distinct spatial states

docs/JBI_POSITIONING_AND_HYPOTHESES.md:13:Flower-colour polymorphism is conventionally defined as the coexistence of at least two discrete flower-colour variants within the same population (Narbona et al. 2018). Reviews of plant balancing selection distinguish mechanisms that maintain variation within populations from mechanisms that maintain differentiation among populations. In particular, negative frequency-dependent selection can maintain within-population polymorphism, whereas spatially varying selection can maintain adaptive differentiation among populations; migration can oppose or redistribute that differentiation (Delph & Kelly 2014).

docs/JBI_POSITIONING_AND_HYPOTHESES.md:19:Flower-colour evolution cannot be reduced to pollinator preference. Narbona et al. (2018) reviewed pollinator selection, non-pollinator selection, genetic drift and gene flow as interacting explanations for flower-colour polymorphism and its geographic variation. Trunschke et al. (2021) further showed that direct evidence for pollinator-mediated selection on flower colour is more limited than is often assumed.

docs/JBI_POSITIONING_AND_HYPOTHESES.md:21:Abiotic and correlated-trait mechanisms are especially relevant for anthocyanin-based systems. Warren & Mackenzie (2001) found morph-by-water-treatment interactions across five polymorphic plant species: pigmented plants performed relatively better under drought whereas unpigmented plants performed relatively better under well-watered conditions. In *Linanthus parryae*, the relative fitness of blue and white morphs changed with annual precipitation, and reciprocal-transplant work linked spatial flower-colour differentiation to local environmental differences (Schemske & Bierzychudek 2001, 2007). In *Boechera stricta*, floral pigmentation was associated with herbivory, elevation and drought; drought induced pigmentation in some white-flowered lineages and white flowers had a fecundity advantage under well-watered conditions (Vaidya et al. 2018).

docs/JBI_POSITIONING_AND_HYPOTHESES.md:41:> Previous work has examined mechanisms maintaining colour polymorphism within populations, geographic variation in morph frequencies, morph-specific climatic niches, and macroecological relationships between flower colour and climate. What has not been directly tested across species is whether **the spatial organization of intraspecific flower-colour variation itself** — local coexistence versus geographic differentiation — is associated with species-level occupied climatic niche breadth.

docs/JBI_POSITIONING_AND_HYPOTHESES.md:61:**Prediction:** within-population polymorphic species should occupy broader climatic niches, whereas geographically structured cases should occur toward the narrower end of species-level occupied climatic breadth.

docs/JBI_POSITIONING_AND_HYPOTHESES.md:102:Moisture has unusually clear biological precedent in anthocyanin-based flower-colour systems: drought-dependent performance differences have been reported across multiple polymorphic species, *Linanthus parryae* shows precipitation-associated temporal and spatial selection, and *Boechera stricta* shows drought-linked pigmentation and fitness trade-offs (Warren & Mackenzie 2001; Schemske & Bierzychudek 2001, 2007; Vaidya et al. 2018).

docs/jbi_cover_letter_template.md:9:Intraspecific phenotypic variation can be maintained as local coexistence or expressed as geographic differentiation, yet comparative studies rarely treat this spatial organization itself as a biogeographic trait. Flower-colour research has established mechanisms maintaining within-population polymorphism, geographic variation in morph frequencies, morph-specific climatic niches, and broad flower colour–climate associations. Our manuscript asks a different cross-species question: **why are colour variants documented as coexisting within populations in some species but geographically differentiated in others, and is that spatial organization associated with species-level occupied climatic niche breadth?**

docs/jbi_cover_letter_template.md:15:We believe the manuscript is particularly suited to *Journal of Biogeography* because the response variable is not flower colour itself but the **spatial organization of intraspecific phenotypic diversity**. The observed direction is not straightforwardly explained by simple broad-gradient climatic sorting and instead identifies a comparative macroecological pattern that motivates future tests of fine-scale environmental variation, biotic interactions, demographic history and migration–selection balance. The paper therefore connects an established evolutionary problem — maintenance versus spatial sorting of polymorphism — with a species-level biogeographic comparison.

docs/jbi_manuscript.md:9:Intraspecific phenotypic variation may be maintained through local coexistence or expressed as geographic differentiation, but comparative studies rarely treat this spatial organization as a distinct trait. We tested whether documented within-population flower-colour polymorphism and geographically structured flower-colour variation differ in species-level occupied climatic niche breadth.
docs/jbi_manuscript.md:31:**Keywords:** climatic niche breadth, evidence synthesis, flower-colour variation, GBIF, geographic differentiation, intraspecific polymorphism, macroecology

docs/jbi_manuscript.md:35:Intraspecific phenotypic variation can be expressed through local coexistence, geographic differentiation or a combination of both. These configurations are biologically distinct because the processes capable of maintaining diversity within a population are not identical to those that maintain differences among populations. Plant balancing-selection theory distinguishes mechanisms such as negative frequency-dependent selection, which can maintain polymorphism within populations, from spatially varying selection, which can maintain adaptive differences among populations when not overwhelmed by migration (Delph & Kelly, 2014). Local coexistence and geographic differentiation can therefore be treated as alternative spatial organizations of intraspecific variation rather than as interchangeable descriptions of the same phenomenon.

docs/jbi_manuscript.md:37:Flower colour provides a tractable system for examining this distinction. Floral pigmentation can affect interactions with pollinators, but colour evolution may also reflect abiotic selection, pleiotropic effects of pigment-pathway genes, genetic drift, gene flow and mating-system processes (Rausher, 2008; Trunschke et al., 2021; Wessinger & Rausher, 2012). Reviews of flower-colour polymorphism emphasize that pollinator-mediated selection is only one component of a broader set of biotic, abiotic and demographic processes, and that the balance among those processes can vary across populations and colour variants (Narbona et al., 2018; Trunschke et al., 2021). Flower colour is therefore both an ecologically meaningful trait and a useful model for asking how intraspecific diversity is arranged geographically.

docs/jbi_manuscript.md:39:Terminology is central to this comparison. Flower-colour polymorphism is conventionally defined as the coexistence of at least two discrete flower-colour variants in the same population (Narbona et al., 2018). We use *intraspecific flower-colour variation* as the umbrella term. *Within-population flower-colour polymorphism* denotes documented local coexistence of discrete variants, whereas *geographically structured flower-colour variation* denotes differentiation among populations or regions without retained evidence of local coexistence. Cases supported at both spatial scales are classified as mixed and do not enter the binary comparison.

docs/jbi_manuscript.md:43:We therefore considered two competing ecological expectations. Under a **broad-gradient environmental-sorting expectation**, species spanning wider macroclimatic conditions provide greater opportunity for spatially varying selection and geographic replacement of colour variants; geographically structured cases could consequently occupy climatic niches at least as broad as, or broader than, within-population cases. Under a **broad-niche coexistence expectation**, inspired by the niche-variation tradition and mechanisms that maintain local polymorphism, broader ecological occupancy may instead accompany the maintenance of multiple phenotypes within populations, predicting broader occupied climatic niches for within-population cases and narrower niches for geographically structured cases (Van Valen, 1965; Delph & Kelly, 2014; Westerband et al., 2021). Neither expectation implies a single causal pathway: geographic differentiation can also arise through fine-scale environmental differences, demographic history, restricted dispersal or drift, whereas local coexistence can reflect frequency dependence, opposing selective agents or microenvironmental heterogeneity.

docs/jbi_manuscript.md:149:The direction of this pattern is ecologically informative because it distinguishes the two expectations posed above. A simple broad-gradient sorting explanation would make geographic differentiation most intuitive when a species spans a broad macroclimatic range across which alternative morphs can be favoured in different places. Morph-level studies demonstrate that such climatic segregation can occur within polymorphic species (Pérez i de Lanuza et al., 2018; Spaseni et al., 2025). In our cross-species comparison, however, geographically structured cases occurred toward the **narrower**, not broader, end of species-level climatic breadth across all five metrics. The result is therefore directionally more compatible with the broad-niche coexistence expectation than with simple broad-gradient climatic sorting. This is a comparison of predictions, not evidence that broad climatic niches themselves maintain polymorphism.

docs/jbi_manuscript.md:153:The contrast among climatic metrics adds ecological resolution without isolating a causal axis. Temperature breadth was weakly associated with spatial organization, whereas moisture breadth produced the largest effect size and PCA hull area the second largest. Moisture has unusually direct precedent in flower-colour ecology. Across five polymorphic plant species, pigmented morphs performed relatively better under drought and unpigmented morphs relatively better under well-watered conditions (Warren & Mackenzie, 2001). Long-term work on *Linanthus parryae* found flower-colour selection that changed through time and space and was associated with precipitation, while reciprocal-transplant work linked local morph advantage with environmental differences (Schemske & Bierzychudek, 2001, 2007). In *Boechera stricta*, drought induced floral pigmentation in white-flowered lineages and white flowers had a fecundity advantage under well-watered conditions, alongside effects of herbivory and elevation (Vaidya et al., 2018). These studies make moisture a biologically plausible axis for follow-up, but our GBIF occurrences are not morph-labelled and our moisture metric describes species-level occupied breadth. Moisture is therefore best treated as a **priority axis for mechanistic testing**, not as an established cause of the spatial pattern observed here.
